compliance.notes: Technically competent, commissioner-overseen TMSS: the core prudential indicators are all present with figures - strongest on capital expenditure/CFR (full year-on-year CFR bridge), the borrowing strategy (clear internal-borrowing/under-borrowing narrative), a properly constructed four-balance liability benchmark chart, the MRP policy statement, and a robust creditworthiness policy using CDS beyond ratings. Weakest area is commercial/non-treasury investment disclosure relative to the size of the legacy 0.9bn book: proportionality is acknowledged but not demonstrated (COM-03 core), the new commercial-income-to-net-revenue indicator is absent (PI-08), and IMPs, the paras 51-53 compliance statement, a quantitative portfolio-risk indicator, an ESG policy, separate HRA/GF benchmarks and an audit-qualification flag are all missing. Overall a compliant recovery-phase strategy whose gaps cluster in the commercial-investment and secondary-disclosure requirements.

gaps.evidence: TMSS s4.4/4.10: 0.9bn commercial initiative caused the intervention and is 'unaffordable in the long term'; being divested
TMSS s16.1-16.2: treasury (financial) investments dealt with in the TMSS, non-financial/service/commercial in the capital strategy

news_drafts.headline: Thurrock's budget depends on emergency government money as asset sales and building programmes slip.
news_drafts.lead: Thurrock Council set a balanced 2026/27 budget only by assuming £68.9m of exceptional financial support from government — money to cover treasury costs and operational deficit that the council cannot otherwise afford. This emergency backing reveals how deeply the authority depends on two promised routes to financial recovery: selling assets and delivering capital projects. Both are failing. The asset disposal programme is on track to raise only £12.2m of a £25.3m budget, a shortfall of 52%. The capital programme, after slipping £87.5m (73% of budget) in 2025/26, is already forecasting a £15.6m underspend (20% of budget) in the first quarter of the new year. Commissioners, who now oversee the council, have required stronger governance and stricter oversight on complex schemes. The council holds reserves to manage pressures but is drawing them down — £17.9m planned for 2026/27 — rather than closing the underlying gap.

news_drafts.headline: Thurrock council's budget depends entirely on £68.9m government emergency support
news_drafts.lead: Thurrock council set its 2026/27 net budget of £267.3m on the assumption of £68.9m of Exceptional Financial Support – a government permission to treat day-to-day spending as capital spending and pay for it through borrowing or asset sales. This represents almost a quarter of the council's total budget. The commissioners' report flagged this dependency as a sustained red risk, noting the council 'remains dependent upon Exceptional Financial Support and the Capitalisation Direction to achieve a balanced budget'. The underlying drivers include the council's inability to deliver capital projects: it underspent its 2025/26 capital budget by £87.5m (73% of the revised total), and is now forecasting that 43 per cent of planned savings will not be achieved. The council is drawing down £17.9m of earmarked reserves during the year to manage current pressures, principally in adult social care.

news_drafts.headline: Thurrock capital programme shows £15.6m underspend in Q1 as commissioners flag risks
news_drafts.lead: Thurrock Council's capital programme is forecast to underspend by £15.6m (20% of its revised first-quarter budget) for 2026/27, repeating failures that prompted commissioners to demand stronger governance and oversight. The council underspent its 2025/26 capital budget by £87.5m (73%). These capital challenges reflect wider financial pressures: the council's savings programme is 43% at risk, with £6.4m of £14.9m targets assessed as unachievable or at risk; Adult Social Care external placements are running £14.4m over budget; and the council remains dependent on £68.9m emergency support via capitalisation direction—permission to finance day-to-day spending by borrowing—to balance its budget.

findings.paper_title: Briefing Note - Corporate and Improvement Plan - 202526 Q4 and End of Year Performance Report and Annual Report - Corporate OS Comments
findings.headline: Agency staffing indicators deteriorating despite improvements in permanent staff recruitment
findings.detail: The scrutiny committee noted a deterioration in the agency staff indicator. Members questioned whether vacancy savings are being offset by higher agency staff costs. Officers highlighted permanent staff improvements but did not directly address the agency cost concern, prompting the committee to request a detailed agency spend report for a future meeting.
findings.matters: Agency staff typically costs 20-30% more than permanent equivalents; deteriorating indicators suggest cost pressures that may undermine savings from improved permanent recruitment
findings.figures: No figures provided in this document
findings.quote: Members queried slippage in divestments and capital investment, along with the deterioration in the agency staff indicator

findings.paper_title: Briefing Note - Corporate and Improvement Plan - 202526 Q4 and End of Year Performance Report and Annual Report - Corporate OS Comments
findings.headline: Capital investment and asset divestment receipts have slipped due to legal processes and factors outside council control
findings.detail: Members queried slippage in both capital investment and divestments. Officers explained delays were due to legal processes and deferred receipts outside the council's control, noting that profiling such slippage across the financial year is not always possible.
findings.matters: Slippage in capital receipts and divestments directly impacts liquidity and funding plans; delays may impair the council's ability to fund planned investment or replace receipts with alternative funding
findings.figures: No figures provided in this document
findings.quote: Delays to divestments were attributed to legal processes and deferred receipts outside the Council's control. Profiling slippage across the year is not always possible.

findings.paper_title: Briefing Note - Corporate and Improvement Plan - 202526 Q4 and End of Year Performance Report and Annual Report - Corporate OS Comments
findings.headline: Thurrock moved from recruitment crisis to stabilisation despite ongoing wage competition from London employers
findings.detail: Officers reported improvements in recruiting and retaining permanent staff through a strengthened senior structure and targeted recruitment. The briefing states that while councils in intervention often face significant recruitment challenges, Thurrock has moved from crisis to stabilisation. However, staff turnover continues due to wage competition from London employers offering higher market rates.
findings.matters: Staffing stability and cost control are essential to financial sustainability; recovery from crisis in a critical area indicates improving operational management and service resilience
findings.figures: No figures provided in this document
findings.quote: While councils in intervention often face significant recruitment challenges, Thurrock has moved from a position of crisis to one of stabilisation.

findings.headline: Council is divesting from its investment portfolio and incurring £1.878m in legal costs to do so.
findings.detail: The Treasury Equalisation Reserve is being drawn down by £1.878m from an opening balance of £6.537m, with this entire drawdown attributed to legal costs of divesting the council's investments. The paper does not explain why the council is exiting its investment portfolio. This represents a material decision to liquidate investments, incurring significant professional fees.
findings.matters: Material investment divestment could indicate either a strategic treasury repositioning or liquidity pressures requiring asset liquidation. For a lender evaluating the council's financial resilience and treasury capacity, this shift warrants investigation into whether it reflects deliberate strategy or financial constraint.
findings.figures: £1.878m drawn from £6.537m opening balance for divestment legal costs; forecast balance £4.659m.
findings.quote: Funding for Legal costs associated with Divestment of the Council's investments

findings.headline: Adult Social Care reserves being heavily drawn down (£9.578m), including a new demographic pressure reserve created in December 2024 that is now entirely exhausted.
findings.detail: The council created an Adult Social Care reserve in December 2024 to fund 'ASC/CS demographic pressures' with an opening balance of £1.500m. This entire reserve is being drawn down in 2026-27. Additionally, the Adult Social Care & Health section is drawing down £8.078m from other established ASC reserves: Better Care Fund (£5.772m), Market Sustainability Funding (£0.693m), ASC - Health integration funding (£1.204m), Adults safeguarding reserve (£0.400m), and ASC grants (£0.009m). This substantial drawdown suggests demographic cost pressures are materialising faster than anticipated.
findings.matters: Adult Social Care is a major service facing demographic pressures from an ageing population. The rapid exhaustion of a reserve created specifically for these pressures just months after establishment signals that ASC cost growth is acute and may force the council to increase levies, reduce services, or seek additional borrowing.
findings.figures: ASC demographic reserve created Dec 2024 with £1.500m: entirely drawn down. Better Care Fund £5.772m drawn; Market Sustainability £0.693m; ASC-Health integration £1.204m; Adults safeguarding £0.400m. Total ASC drawdown £9.578m from starting balance of £17.205m.
findings.quote: New Reserve created for ASC/CS demographic pressures as agreed at December 2024 Cabinet
